Let \(p=d_2\) be the smallest prime divisor of \(n\). Then \(x=p-1\), and from the condition
\[
d_j=1+(p-1)\frac{j(j-1)}2.
\]
For each \(2\le j\le k-1\), since \(d_j\mid n\), we have
\[
d_j \mid n-d_j=(p-1)\left(\frac{k(k-1)}2-\frac{j(j-1)}2\right).
\]
But \(\gcd(d_j,p-1)=1\), so
\[
d_j \mid \frac{k(k-1)}2-\frac{j(j-1)}2.
\]
Taking \(j=k-1\),
\[
d_{k-1}\mid k-1.
\]
Since divisors are increasing positive integers, \(d_{k-1}\ge k-1\), hence
\[
d_{k-1}=k-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
1+(p-1)\frac{(k-1)(k-2)}2=k-1,
\]
so
\[
(p-1)\frac{(k-1)(k-2)}2=k-2.
\]
If \(k=3\), this gives \(p-1=1\), so \(p=2\), and
\[
n=d_3=1+1\cdot 3=4.
\]
If \(k>3\), dividing by \(k-2\) gives
\[
\frac{(p-1)(k-1)}2=1,
\]
impossible since \(p\ge 2\) and \(k-1\ge 3\).

Thus the only composite positive integer is
\[
\boxed{4}.
\]
